title: Human Approval for AI Agents: What Needs a Person's Yes
dek: Human approval for AI agents keeps costly mistakes from going out the door. Here is which agent actions need a person's yes, and how to keep it fast.
keywords: when should AI agents ask permission
summary: Human approval for AI agents means a person signs off before an agent takes an action that is hard to undo, like sending to a client, spending money or publishing. Agents can be confidently wrong about context they were never given. A short, named review step catches those mistakes without losing the speed.

hero.alt: A 1930s pulp noir illustration of Momo the robot mascot as a newspaper editor at a cluttered desk, one arm raised holding a large blank rubber stamp

body.heading: Why does human approval still matter when AI agents do the work?
paragraphs: Human approval matters because AI agents can be confidently wrong, and some mistakes are expensive to undo. A wrong claim in a client email, an ad budget set too high or a post that misstates a price cannot be pulled back once it is out.
This guide is for small business owners and marketing teams who use AI agents, or plan to, and want a clear rule for what the agent can do alone and what waits for a person.
The goal is not to slow agents down. It is to put a person exactly where judgment matters and nowhere else.

subsections.heading: What human approval means
paragraphs: Human approval is a checkpoint where an agent stops, shows a person what it plans to do, and waits for a yes before acting. People also call this human in the loop.
The agent still does the research, the drafting and the busywork. The person makes the final call on the few actions that carry real risk.

subsections.heading: Why it matters more as agents do more
paragraphs: A chatbot only suggests text, so a person always takes the last step by hand. An agent can take that step itself, such as sending the email or changing the bid, which is exactly why the checkpoint has to be designed on purpose.

body.heading: What do AI agents actually get wrong?
paragraphs: Agents rarely get grammar or tone wrong. What they miss is context nobody gave them.

subsections.heading: Missing context
paragraphs: An agent may not know that a promotion ended last week, that a customer asked not to be emailed, or that a phrase reads badly for one specific audience. A new hire in their first week makes the same kind of mistake.

subsections.heading: Confident tone
paragraphs: An agent often sounds just as sure when it is wrong as when it is right. It does not hesitate the way a careful person might, so the tone of a draft is no signal of its accuracy.

subsections.heading: Over-literal goals
paragraphs: Agents can take a goal further than you meant. Anthropic's [framework for safe and trustworthy agents](https://www.anthropic.com/news/our-framework-for-developing-safe-and-trustworthy-agents) gives the example of an agent asked to organize files that deletes what it thinks are duplicates and restructures the whole system.

subsections.heading: Speed
paragraphs: The difference from a new hire is speed. An agent can produce a confident, wrong result far faster than a person, so the review step has to keep pace.

subsections.heading: Stale information
paragraphs: Agents work from whatever data they were given or can find, and that data can be out of date. An agent may quote last season's hours, an old price list or a staff member who has left.
A person who knows the business spots those errors in seconds. That is a big part of why the final check belongs to someone close to the work.

body.heading: Which AI agent actions need a person's yes?
paragraphs: Any action that is hard or costly to undo needs a person's yes. Most teams can sort their agent work into three groups.

subsections.heading: Always needs approval
paragraphs: Sending anything to a client or customer list, spending money, changing a live ad campaign, publishing to a website or social account, and deleting data. These are the actions where a mistake reaches the real world.

subsections.heading: Light check
paragraphs: Internal drafts, research summaries and first versions of reports. A quick skim on a normal schedule is enough, since mistakes here cost little to fix.

subsections.heading: No approval needed
paragraphs: Reading files, gathering public data, resizing images or formatting a spreadsheet. These actions change nothing outside the agent's own workspace.

subsections.heading: How the big platforms handle it
paragraphs: AI companies build this split into their own tools. OpenAI's [production notes for GPT Actions](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/actions/production) let builders flag an action as consequential, such as booking and paying for a hotel room, so ChatGPT always asks the user to confirm before running it. Anthropic notes that Claude Code reads by default but asks for approval before actions that modify code or systems.

subsections.heading: Approval by job type
paragraphs: For client email, approve the final draft and the recipient list. For ads, approve budget, bid and new campaign changes, while letting the agent pull reports freely.

For social posts, approve the post and the image before it is scheduled. For website changes, approve anything that goes live, while letting the agent prepare drafts on a staging copy. Our look at [a day in the life of AI marketing agents](/daily/ai-marketing-agents-day-in-the-life) walks through where these checkpoints fall in a normal workday.

body.heading: Human approval makes sense if, and when to loosen it
paragraphs: Strict approval makes sense when the action touches money, customers, public channels or data you cannot recover. It also makes sense for a new agent, a new client or a new type of task, when nobody knows the agent's habits yet.
You can loosen the review, not remove it, when an agent has a long clean record on a narrow, repeatable task. A weekly report built from the same data source every week is a good example.

Keep the rule written down. The [NIST AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework) is a voluntary guide, but its core idea applies to a five person shop too: decide who is accountable for each AI system before something goes wrong.

body.heading: How do you keep approval fast instead of a bottleneck?
paragraphs: Approval is fast when the agent hands over finished work with its reasoning attached. A person then checks the right things instead of redoing the research.

subsections.heading: A good handoff
paragraphs: The draft should show its sources, state what it assumed and flag anything it was unsure about. Our guide on [how AI agents hand work to people](/daily/how-ai-agents-hand-work-to-people) shows what a clean handoff looks like.

subsections.heading: A named owner
paragraphs: Every approval type needs one person who owns it. An unassigned review gets skipped on a busy day.

subsections.heading: Clear checkpoints
paragraphs: Anthropic's guide to [building effective agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents) describes agents that pause for human feedback at checkpoints or when they hit a blocker. Put the checkpoint right before the risky action, not after every small step.

subsections.heading: What an approval request should include
paragraphs: A good request fits on one screen. It says what the agent wants to do, who it affects, what it will cost if anything, the sources behind any claims, and what the agent was unsure about.

For example, an agent proposing an ad budget change should show the current budget, the new budget, the reason, and the last two weeks of results it based the change on. The approver can then say yes or no in a minute.

subsections.heading: Batching
paragraphs: Group routine approvals into one or two set times a day. A reviewer who clears ten small requests at once moves faster than one who is interrupted ten times.

body.heading: What are the most common approval mistakes?
paragraphs: The first mistake is reviewing everything the same way. When every draft gets the same heavy review, people start skimming, and the risky ones slip through.
The second is skipping review because the agent has been reliable. Track record should change how carefully you read, not whether you read.

The third is approving without context. If the reviewer cannot see the sources or the agent's assumptions, the yes is a guess. The fourth is never updating the rule when a new client, channel or agent arrives.

subsections.heading: Rubber stamping
paragraphs: When approvals pile up, reviewers start clicking yes without reading. That is worse than no review, because everyone assumes someone checked.
Keep the always approve list short so each request gets real attention. If the list grows past what one person can read carefully, split ownership.

subsections.heading: No record of the yes
paragraphs: If nobody records who approved what, a mistake turns into a guessing game. A simple log with the action, the approver and the time is enough.
That log also shows which agents earn a lighter review over time, because you can see their record instead of relying on memory.

body.heading: A simple worked example
paragraphs: Here is an example with made up numbers to show the trade, not a measured result. Say writing a client newsletter by hand takes a marketer 3 hours.

With an agent, the research and first draft take the marketer 0 hours of their own time. Reviewing a draft that shows its sources takes about 20 minutes, so the marketer saves about 2 hours and 40 minutes per newsletter.

Now say 1 newsletter in 20 would have gone out with a wrong claim. Across 20 newsletters, review costs about 6 hours and 40 minutes in total and catches that one mistake before it reaches the client's whole list. Compared with 60 hours of hand writing, the team still saves over 53 hours.

body.heading: How should a small business set up its approval rules?
paragraphs: Step 1: Write down every action your agents can take. Step 2: Mark each one as always approve, light check or no approval, using the undo test. Step 3: Name one owner for each always approve action.
Step 4: Require every agent draft to include sources, assumptions and open questions. Step 5: Review the list each quarter, and any time you add a new client, channel or agent.

If you are still choosing tools, read our comparison of [AI agents vs chatbots](/daily/ai-agents-vs-chatbots) and our checklist for [keeping client data safe with AI tools](/daily/client-data-safe-ai-tools). At Momentum we run our own agents on this same rule: the agent drafts, a person approves anything that leaves the building.

faq.question: Should every AI generated draft get a full human review?
faq.answer: No. Match the review to the risk: light checks for internal drafts, full review for anything that reaches a client, spends money or goes public.

faq.question: Does human review cancel out the time AI agents save?
faq.answer: No. The agent still does the slow research and drafting, and reviewing a finished draft with sources usually takes minutes, not hours.

faq.question: What is human in the loop for AI agents?
faq.answer: It means a person is part of the workflow at set points, usually approving actions before they happen. The agent works on its own between those checkpoints.

faq.question: Can an AI agent ever approve its own work?
faq.answer: It can check its own work, but it should not give the final yes on actions that are hard to undo. That call belongs to a named person.

faq.question: Who should approve AI agent actions in a small team?
faq.answer: The person who would answer for the mistake, such as the account owner for client sends or the budget owner for ad spend. Name them in writing.

takeaways: The simplest approval rule is to ask how hard an action would be to undo, and require a person's yes for anything expensive to take back.
AI agent builders already work this way: Anthropic says humans should retain control before high-stakes decisions are made.
Review is fast when the agent hands over sources, assumptions and open questions along with the draft.
Approval only works when one named person owns it for each type of action.
A good track record earns an agent a faster review, never a skipped one.
